findings: 2026-11-06: drafted for Mathematics 12 Unit 3 (owner request): English and a teacher-style Roman Urdu lesson; the book's content in order with our clearly labelled teaching notes; worked examples step by step with reasons; results verified with sympy.

Book correction: The book prints the total distance as \int_{t_2}^{t_1} v(t)\,dt: the limits are upside down and the modulus is missing. As the sentence before it says, the distance is the integral of the speed |v(t)|: total distance traveled = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v(t)|\,dt.

Book correction: The second line prints \text{Distance} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,dt, which is the same integral as the displacement. It should be \text{Distance} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v(t)|\,dt = A_1 + A_2 + A_3: taking |v| turns the part below the axis upwards, so A_2 is added instead of subtracted.

Book correction: The book writes v(t) = \int_{0}^{t} a(t)\,dt = \dots + c. A definite integral from 0 to t has no constant of integration; it gives v(t) - v(0), not v(t). Correct: v(t) = \int a(t)\,dt = 3t^{2} - 18t + c (an indefinite integral), or equivalently v(t) = v(0) + \int_{0}^{t} a(u)\,du. Both give v(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 15, so the book's answer is right.
